clue.text: Demonstrator's fall

definitions.meaning: a demonstrator is one who shows something, so the word can be read as 'one who shows'; the 's stands for 'is'
a brief fall of rain or snow

explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, the word names a person who shows things, a demonstrator; it is also a short burst of rain.

clue.text: Oh. I get along smashing windows.

definitions.text: Oh. I get along smashing windows.

indicators.note: the letters of 'Oh I' and 'along' are smashed up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A vandal cheerfully remarks that he is getting on fine breaking glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smashing' rearranges OHI plus ALONG; 'get' only links. The whole clue is also the vandal speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A thug who breaks windows for fun is a typical young vandal.

clue.text: Bird from the island, what about that?

indicators.note: one word goes around the other, as 'about' means surrounding

parts.note: an inch is a small island in Scotland, as in Inchcolm

explanation.surface: Someone spots a bird from an island and exclaims at it.
explanation.walkthrough: INCH is a Scottish word for a small island; WHAT goes around it.
explanation.definitionFit: The whinchat is a small brown songbird of heaths and grassland.

clue.text: Give up holding John Anderson, I reply

indicators.note: the word for 'give up' holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: to render is to give up or hand over
Burns' song begins 'John Anderson, my jo', jo being Scots for sweetheart

explanation.surface: A man refuses to keep John Anderson and answers personally.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns' poem 'John Anderson, my jo, John' addresses him as 'jo', a Scots word for darling.
explanation.definitionFit: A rejoinder is a sharp answer, a retort.

clue.text: The standard tirade-it's outrageous!

parts.note: a standard is a flag carried as an emblem
a tirade is an angry rant

explanation.surface: Someone holds up a banner and launches into an outraged speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Flagrant behaviour is shockingly open and scandalous, i.e. outrageous.

clue.text: Did. Ruler of the Queen's Navee, as office boy, rise thus in a rage.?

definitions.text: Did. Ruler of the Queen's Navee, as office boy, rise thus in a rage.?

parts.words: Did. Ruler of the Queen's Navee, as office boy, rise thus in a rage.?
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore, Sir Joseph rose to rule the navy after polishing up the brass knob of the big front door as an office boy; to lose one's temper uses that knob

explanation.surface: Gilbert and Sullivan's First Lord of the Admiralty is pictured rising from office boy in a temper.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR's stray full stops are not printed; the clue asks whether Sir Joseph Porter rose 'off' the knob he polished.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose one's temper suddenly is the idiom, while the office boy literally rose from polishing the door's knob.

clue.text: Superfluous to pick holes in Swiss dairy product

definitions.text: Superfluous to pick holes in Swiss dairy product

parts.words: Superfluous to pick holes in Swiss dairy product
parts.note: to pick holes is to find fault, but a Swiss cheese already has holes, so making more is needless

explanation.definitionFit: A hard Swiss cheese known for its holes is the dairy product one needn't make holes in.

clue.text: One's entitled to get it on tap

definitions.text: One's entitled to get it on tap

parts.words: One's entitled to get it on tap
parts.note: a person given a title, a knight, receives a tap of the sword on the shoulder, not a drink from a tap

explanation.definitionFit: The ceremonial touch of a sword that confers knighthood is the honour received by one given a title.

clue.text: Took a chance with the flip side

definitions.text: Took a chance with the flip side

parts.words: Took a chance with the flip side
parts.note: decided by flipping a coin and gambling on which side lands up

explanation.definitionFit: Flipping a coin to decide something means leaving the outcome to chance.

clue.text: Sort of 15 ac, to call casually with a bird

parts.note: to pop in is to drop by on someone informally
the jay is a crow-family bird

explanation.surface: A dandy drops by casually, accompanied by a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 across is KNUT, an old word for a showy dandy; a popinjay is a vain, foppish person of the same sort.
explanation.definitionFit: A popinjay is a vain, overdressed show-off, the same kind of person as a knut or fop.

clue.text: Doctors are phoneys we hear from Donald

definitions.meaning: charlatan doctors who only pretend to medical skill
the noises made by Donald Duck, the cartoon character

explanation.surface: Sham physicians and a cartoon duck share a description.
explanation.definitionFit: Fraudulent medics are called by the same word as the calls a duck makes, and Donald Duck is the cartoon bird.

clue.text: Devilish work found for the unemployed

definitions.text: Devilish work found for the unemployed

parts.words: Devilish work found for the unemployed
parts.note: plays on the proverb that the devil finds work for idle hands: the 'unemployed' are the idle

explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says Satan finds wrongdoing for idle hands, so naughty trouble-making is the devil's work for the idle.

clue.text: Corn in some alien field

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words 'some alien', running across the gap between them

explanation.surface: Maize is growing in a strange foreign field.
explanation.walkthrough: A mealie is South African English for an ear of maize, called corn in North America.
explanation.definitionFit: In South Africa maize is called mealies, so a single cob of that cereal is a mealie.

clue.text: Evita did turn out to be something extra

indicators.note: to turn out is to come out differently, so the letters of 'Evita did' are rearranged

explanation.surface: The musical Evita turned out to be a bonus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn out' rearranges EVITADID into the answer; Evita is the Lloyd Webber musical.
explanation.definitionFit: An additive is a substance put in on top of the main ingredients, an extra.

clue.text: Scathing description of uncontrolled civil riot

indicators.note: an uncontrolled riot runs wild, so its letters with 'civil' are scrambled

explanation.surface: A harsh account is given of a disorderly street riot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncontrolled' rearranges CIVILRIOT; 'description of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Vitriolic words are as caustic as sulphuric acid, i.e. bitterly scathing.

clue.text: King joins the teachers, smart man !

parts.note: K is the chess and card abbreviation for king
NUT is the National Union of Teachers, a British teaching union

explanation.surface: A monarch becomes a member of the teachers' union, the dapper fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: A knut (the K is sounded or silent) is an Edwardian slang word for a fashionable young dandy, so 'smart' means well dressed, not clever.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edwardian slang word named a fashionable, dapper young fellow, a man who was smart in dress.

clue.text: Royal mail on the beam?

parts.note: a king is royal, the head of a royal house
post is mail, letters delivered

explanation.surface: Royal Mail deliveries are on track.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal Mail is Britain's postal service; the surface hints at it, but the two words split into separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A kingpost is the upright central timber in a roof truss, a structural beam.

clue.text: Hold-up during a 1

parts.note: 1 across is a fall of rain; the thing held up over one's head during it is wanted, not a robbery

explanation.definitionFit: A folding canopy carried overhead keeps off rain, so it is held up in a downpour.

clue.text: Spring, this year

definitions.meaning: the puzzle appeared in a year with 29 February, a year with an extra day

explanation.definitionFit: A jump is a spring, and a year of 366 days takes the same name, which the setter says the current year was.

clue.text: Plucky Australian flier ?

parts.note: 'plucky' suggests bravery, but the bird is named for the plucked stringed instrument its tail resembles

explanation.definitionFit: An Australian bird whose spread tail looks like the harp-like instrument played by plucking.

clue.text: Only men get in at the junction

indicators.note: the first pieces get in between the letters of 'at'

parts.note: but means only, as in 'but a child'

explanation.surface: Only men are admitted at the meeting point.
explanation.walkthrough: An abutment is the point where two things meet, as where a bridge rests on its support.
explanation.definitionFit: An abutment is a meeting point where two structures touch, so a junction.

clue.text: Ministerial reply, it's out of order

indicators.note: letters out of their order are muddled, so 'reply' and 'it's' are rearranged together

parts.note: the apostrophe is dropped, leaving the three letters as written

explanation.surface: A government minister's answer is ruled out of order in the chamber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of order' rearranges REPLY plus ITS. 'Ministerial' looks political, but here it means belonging to a minister of religion.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister of religion is a clergyman, so something ministerial in that sense is clerical, befitting a cleric.

clue.text: Where a Sicilian doctor lost his tan?

parts.note: someone who has lost his tan is paler
MO is Medical Officer, an army doctor

explanation.surface: A Sicilian doctor wonders where his suntan went.
explanation.walkthrough: Palermo is the capital of Sicily, so it is where a Sicilian may live.
explanation.definitionFit: Palermo is the chief city of Sicily, a natural home for an islander.

clue.text: Misrepresent dress, having the French style

parts.note: garb is clothing or dress
le is the French masculine word for 'the'

explanation.surface: Someone distorts the facts about a frock made in Gallic style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' joins the two pieces and 'style' only finishes the surface picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To garble an account is to distort it, so that it gives a false picture.

clue.text: One put in advance payment for, liqueur

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the stake named by 'advance payment'

parts.note: an ante is a stake paid in before cards are dealt in poker
I is the Roman numeral one
to set something is to put it down

explanation.surface: Someone pays up front for an after-dinner drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Anisette is a sweet aniseed-flavoured cordial, one of the classic liqueurs.

clue.text: Home for Pooh's 'learned friend (spelling corrected)

parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh's wise friend is the bird who misspells his own name WOL; corrected, it gives the bird, and a home for those birds is wanted

explanation.definitionFit: A dwelling for nocturnal birds of prey is named from the bird with the suffix for a place where creatures are kept.

clue.text: Musical instrument to cure mild disorder

indicators.note: putting letters into disorder jumbles 'cure mild' into a new word

explanation.surface: A tune played on an instrument is prescribed to cure a minor ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disorder' looks like the illness, but it is the signal to rearrange CUREMILD.
explanation.definitionFit: The dulcimer is a stringed instrument played with small hammers.

clue.text: Leaves much to be desired here in the East

definitions.text: Leaves much to be desired here in the East

parts.words: Leaves much to be desired here in the East
parts.note: 'leaves' are tea leaves, eagerly wanted at an oriental establishment that serves the brew

explanation.definitionFit: An Eastern café where the drink brewed from leaves is served is where those leaves are in demand.

clue.text: Forces students who are less likely to succeed

definitions.meaning: trainees for the armed forces, at a military academy or in school corps

definitions.text: who are less likely to succeed
definitions.meaning: younger sons, who traditionally did not inherit the family title or estate

explanation.definitionFit: Military trainees share the name with younger sons, who stood behind the eldest in line to succeed to an inheritance.
